title: Modular Arithmetic and Congruence
summary: Modular arithmetic is arithmetic of remainders: numbers "wrap around" after reaching a fixed modulus, exactly like hours on a clock or days of a week. This chapter covers the mod operation, congruence modulo n, its properties, modular inverses, linear congruences and everyday applications such as clocks, calendars and unit digits of large powers.

notes.heading: The division algorithm and a mod n
notes.html:
For any integer a and any positive integer n there are unique integers q (quotient) and r (remainder) such that a = nq + r, where 0 ≤ r < n. This is the division algorithm.

The remainder r is written a mod n and read "a modulo n". The number n is called the modulus.

  • 47 mod 6 = 5, because 47 = 6 × 7 + 5.
  • 30 mod 5 = 0, because 5 divides 30 exactly.
  • For a negative number the remainder must still lie between 0 and n − 1: −17 = 5 × (−4) + 3, so −17 mod 5 = 3 (not −2).

So a mod n can only take the n values 0, 1, 2, …, n − 1. This set is called the set of least non-negative residues modulo n, written Zn.

notes.heading: Congruence modulo n
notes.html:
Two integers a and b are congruent modulo n if they leave the same remainder when divided by n. Equivalently, n divides their difference:

a ≡ b (mod n) ⇔ n | (a − b) ⇔ a − b = kn for some integer k.

  • 38 ≡ 14 (mod 6) because 38 − 14 = 24 = 6 × 4.
  • 25 ≢ 4 (mod 6) because 25 − 4 = 21 is not a multiple of 6.
  • −7 ≡ 5 (mod 12) because −7 − 5 = −12. (7 hours before midnight is 5 o'clock.)

Congruence is an equivalence relation: it is reflexive (a ≡ a), symmetric (a ≡ b ⇒ b ≡ a) and transitive (a ≡ b and b ≡ c ⇒ a ≡ c). It splits all integers into n classes, called residue classes or congruence classes.

notes.heading: Properties of congruence (rules of modular arithmetic)
notes.html:
If a ≡ b (mod n) and c ≡ d (mod n), then:

  1. a + c ≡ b + d (mod n) — congruences can be added.
  2. a − c ≡ b − d (mod n) — congruences can be subtracted.
  3. ac ≡ bd (mod n) — congruences can be multiplied.
  4. ak ≡ bk (mod n) for every positive integer k — congruences can be raised to powers.
  5. a + m ≡ b + m and am ≡ bm (mod n) for any integer m.

In practice: (a + b) mod n = [(a mod n) + (b mod n)] mod n and (a × b) mod n = [(a mod n) × (b mod n)] mod n. So we may replace any number by its remainder at any stage — this keeps the numbers small.

Caution: congruences cannot in general be divided. 2 × 3 ≡ 2 × 8 (mod 10) (6 ≡ 16) but 3 ≢ 8 (mod 10). Cancellation of a common factor k is allowed only when gcd(k, n) = 1.

notes.heading: Additive and multiplicative inverses; linear congruences
notes.html:
Additive inverse of a modulo n is the number b in Zn with a + b ≡ 0 (mod n). Example: the additive inverse of 9 mod 13 is 4, since 9 + 4 = 13 ≡ 0.

Multiplicative inverse of a modulo n is the number a−1 with a × a−1 ≡ 1 (mod n). It exists only when gcd(a, n) = 1. Example: 4−1 mod 11 = 3, since 4 × 3 = 12 ≡ 1 (mod 11). 2 has no inverse mod 6 because gcd(2, 6) = 2.

A linear congruence is ax ≡ b (mod n). Key result: it has a solution if and only if d = gcd(a, n) divides b, and then it has exactly d incongruent solutions modulo n.

Method to solve ax ≡ b (mod n):

  1. Find d = gcd(a, n). If d does not divide b, there is no solution.
  2. If d > 1, divide a, b and n by d to get a'x ≡ b' (mod n').
  3. Find the inverse of a' modulo n' (by trial: a' × 1, a' × 2, … until the product leaves remainder 1).
  4. Multiply both sides by the inverse: x ≡ (inverse × b') mod n'.
  5. If d > 1, list the d solutions x, x + n', x + 2n', … below n. Check one solution by substitution.

notes.heading: Worked Example 1 — remainder of a large power
notes.html:
Find the remainder when 3100 is divided by 7.

Step 1: Find the cycle of powers of 3 modulo 7:

k123456
3k mod 7326451

(32 = 9 ≡ 2; 33 ≡ 2 × 3 = 6; 34 ≡ 6 × 3 = 18 ≡ 4; 35 ≡ 12 ≡ 5; 36 ≡ 15 ≡ 1.)

Step 2: Since 36 ≡ 1 (mod 7), write 100 = 6 × 16 + 4.

Step 3: 3100 = (36)16 × 34 ≡ 116 × 4 = 4 (mod 7).

Remainder = 4.

notes.heading: Worked Example 2 — clocks, calendars and unit digits
notes.html:
(a) It is 9 o'clock now (12-hour clock). What time will it show after 50 hours?

Hours on a dial work modulo 12: (9 + 50) mod 12 = 59 mod 12 = 11 (since 59 = 12 × 4 + 11). The clock shows 11 o'clock.

(b) Today is Monday. Which day will it be after 100 days?

Days repeat modulo 7: 100 = 7 × 14 + 2, so 100 ≡ 2 (mod 7). Two days after Monday is Wednesday.

(c) Find the unit digit of 72025.

The unit digit is the remainder mod 10. Powers of 7 mod 10: 7, 9, 3, 1, then repeat (cycle length 4). 2025 = 4 × 506 + 1, so 72025 ≡ 71 = 7 (mod 10). Unit digit = 7.

notes.heading: Worked Example 3 — solving linear congruences
notes.html:
(a) Solve 3x ≡ 4 (mod 7).

gcd(3, 7) = 1, so there is exactly one solution mod 7. Inverse of 3 mod 7: 3 × 5 = 15 ≡ 1, so 3−1 = 5.

Multiply both sides by 5: x ≡ 20 ≡ 6 (mod 7). Check: 3 × 6 = 18 = 14 + 4 ≡ 4 ✓. x ≡ 6 (mod 7), i.e. x = 6, 13, 20, …

(b) Solve 4x ≡ 6 (mod 10).

d = gcd(4, 10) = 2 and 2 | 6, so there are 2 solutions mod 10. Divide by 2: 2x ≡ 3 (mod 5). Inverse of 2 mod 5 is 3 (2 × 3 = 6 ≡ 1). x ≡ 9 ≡ 4 (mod 5).

Solutions mod 10: x = 4 and x = 4 + 5 = 9. Check: 4 × 4 = 16 ≡ 6 ✓; 4 × 9 = 36 ≡ 6 ✓. x ≡ 4 or 9 (mod 10).

(c) Solve 6x ≡ 5 (mod 9). gcd(6, 9) = 3 does not divide 5, so there is no solution.

notes.heading: Common mistakes to avoid
notes.html:
• Giving a negative remainder: −23 mod 5 is 2, not −3. Always add the modulus until the answer lies in 0 to n − 1.
  • Dividing both sides of a congruence by a number that shares a factor with the modulus.
  • Forgetting that a multiplicative inverse exists only when gcd(a, n) = 1.
  • For days of the week, counting the starting day as day 1. "After 100 days" means add 100 to today, then reduce mod 7.
  • For a 24-hour clock use mod 24; for a dial clock use mod 12 and remember that remainder 0 means 12 o'clock.
  • Saying a linear congruence has one solution when gcd(a, n) = d > 1 — it has d solutions.

keyTerms.definition: The fixed positive integer n with respect to which remainders are taken in a ≡ b (mod n).
The remainder r (0 ≤ r < n) left when a is divided by n.
a ≡ b (mod n) means n divides a − b, i.e. a and b leave the same remainder on division by n.
The set of all integers congruent to a given number modulo n; there are exactly n such classes.
The set {0, 1, 2, …, n − 1} of least non-negative residues modulo n.
The number b with a + b ≡ 0 (mod n); it equals n − (a mod n) when a is not a multiple of n.
The number a<sup>−1</sup> with a × a<sup>−1</sup> ≡ 1 (mod n); it exists only when gcd(a, n) = 1.
A congruence of the form ax ≡ b (mod n); solvable iff gcd(a, n) divides b.
The repeating pattern of remainders of successive powers a, a<sup>2</sup>, a<sup>3</sup>, … modulo n, used for large powers.

formulas.name: Division algorithm
formulas.html: a = nq + r, 0 ≤ r < n; r = a mod n

formulas.name: Definition of congruence
formulas.html: a ≡ b (mod n) ⇔ n | (a − b) ⇔ a mod n = b mod n

formulas.name: Addition rule
formulas.html: (a + b) mod n = [(a mod n) + (b mod n)] mod n

formulas.name: Subtraction rule
formulas.html: (a − b) mod n = [(a mod n) − (b mod n) + n] mod n

formulas.name: Multiplication rule
formulas.html: (a × b) mod n = [(a mod n) × (b mod n)] mod n

formulas.name: Power rule
formulas.html: a ≡ b (mod n) ⇒ a<sup>k</sup> ≡ b<sup>k</sup> (mod n)

formulas.name: Using a cycle
formulas.html: If a<sup>m</sup> ≡ 1 (mod n) and k = mq + s, then a<sup>k</sup> ≡ a<sup>s</sup> (mod n)

formulas.name: Additive inverse
formulas.html: −a mod n = n − (a mod n), when a mod n ≠ 0

formulas.name: Multiplicative inverse
formulas.html: a × a<sup>−1</sup> ≡ 1 (mod n), exists iff gcd(a, n) = 1

formulas.name: Linear congruence
formulas.html: ax ≡ b (mod n) solvable iff d = gcd(a, n) | b; then d solutions mod n

formulas.name: Clock / calendar
formulas.html: Dial clock: mod 12; 24-hour clock: mod 24; day of week: mod 7; unit digit: mod 10

mcqs.q: It is 7 a.m. now. What time will it be 75 hours later?
mcqs.explanation: Use mod 24: 75 = 24 × 3 + 3. So the time is 3 hours after 7 a.m., i.e. 10 a.m. (three days later).

mcqs.explanation: We need b with 9 + b ≡ 0 (mod 13): b = 13 − 9 = 4. (−9 is not an element of Z<sub>13</sub>.)

Assertion (A): The congruence 7x ≡ 2 (mod 14) has no solution.
Reason (R): ax ≡ b (mod n) has a solution if and only if gcd(a, n) divides b.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcqs.explanation: R is the standard theorem. gcd(7, 14) = 7 and 7 does not divide 2, so by R there is no solution — A is true and follows from R.

mcqs.q: Today is Friday. Which day of the week will it be after 1000 days?
mcqs.explanation: 1000 = 7 × 142 + 6, so 1000 ≡ 6 (mod 7). Six days after Friday is Thursday.

questions.q: Find the remainder when 5<sup>40</sup> is divided by 6.
A wall clock (12-hour dial) shows 4 o'clock. What will it show after 1000 hours?
questions.answerHtml:
Dial positions repeat every 12 hours, so work modulo 12.

(4 + 1000) mod 12 = 1004 mod 12. Since 1004 = 12 × 83 + 8, the remainder is 8.

The clock will show 8 o'clock.

questions.q: Solve the linear congruence 4x ≡ 6 (mod 10) and list all incongruent solutions.
questions.answerHtml:
Step 1: d = gcd(4, 10) = 2, and 2 divides 6, so there are exactly 2 solutions modulo 10.

Step 2: Divide by 2: 2x ≡ 3 (mod 5).

Step 3: Inverse of 2 modulo 5 is 3, because 2 × 3 = 6 ≡ 1 (mod 5). Multiply: x ≡ 9 ≡ 4 (mod 5).

Step 4: Solutions modulo 10 are x = 4 and x = 4 + 5 = 9.

Check: 4 × 4 = 16 ≡ 6 (mod 10) ✓ and 4 × 9 = 36 ≡ 6 (mod 10) ✓.

x ≡ 4 (mod 10) or x ≡ 9 (mod 10).

questions.q: Using congruences, prove that 2<sup>3n</sup> − 1 is divisible by 7 for every natural number n.
questions.answerHtml:
23n = (23)n = 8n.

Since 8 = 7 + 1, we have 8 ≡ 1 (mod 7).

By the power rule, 8n ≡ 1n = 1 (mod 7).

Hence 23n − 1 ≡ 1 − 1 = 0 (mod 7), i.e. 7 divides 23n − 1 for every natural n. ∎

questions.q: (a) Find the remainder when 17<sup>23</sup> is divided by 5. (b) Find the unit digit of 17<sup>23</sup>. (c) Find x in Z<sub>9</sub> such that 7x ≡ 1 (mod 9).
questions.answerHtml:
(a) 17 ≡ 2 (mod 5). Powers of 2 mod 5: 2, 4, 3, 1 (cycle of 4). 23 = 4 × 5 + 3, so 1723 ≡ 223 ≡ 23 = 8 ≡ 3 (mod 5). Remainder = 3.

(b) 17 ≡ 7 (mod 10). Unit digits of powers of 7: 7, 9, 3, 1 (cycle of 4). 23 ≡ 3 (mod 4), so the unit digit is the third term, 3. (Consistent with (a): a number ending in 3 leaves remainder 3 on division by 5.)

(c) gcd(7, 9) = 1, so an inverse exists. Try multiples of 7: 7 × 1 = 7, 7 × 2 = 14 ≡ 5, 7 × 3 = 21 ≡ 3, 7 × 4 = 28 ≡ 1 (mod 9). x = 4.

questions.q:
Case study. A cargo ship leaves port at 22:00 hours (24-hour clock) on a Tuesday. Its voyage takes 150 hours. A second ship leaves at the same time on a voyage of 100 hours. The port crane is serviced every 9 days, and was last serviced on that Tuesday.
(i) At what time and on which day does the first ship arrive?
(ii) At what time and on which day does the second ship arrive?
(iii) On which day of the week will the 10th service after that Tuesday fall?
questions.answerHtml:
(i) Hours counted from 00:00 Tuesday: 22 + 150 = 172. 172 = 24 × 7 + 4, so 172 ≡ 4 (mod 24): the clock shows 04:00. Seven full days have passed, and 7 ≡ 0 (mod 7), so the day is again Tuesday (of the next week).

(ii) 22 + 100 = 122 = 24 × 5 + 2. Time = 02:00; 5 days after Tuesday is Sunday.

(iii) The 10th service comes 10 × 9 = 90 days later. 90 = 7 × 12 + 6, so 90 ≡ 6 (mod 7). Six days after Tuesday is Monday.
